claim: Article 15(3): nothing in Article 15 stops the State from making any special provision for women and children. (Article 15(1) bars discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth: ledger POL03-B04.)
value: special provision for women allowed
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Text for 15(3) is in ledger POL03-B05 too; this row pins the PDF page. Courts read 15(3) as enabling real benefits, not stereotypes (see Anuj Garg, claim -10).

claim: Directive Principles on sex equality: Article 39(a) men and women equally have the right to an adequate means of livelihood; 39(d) equal pay for equal work for both men and women; 39(e) the health and strength of workers, men and women, not to be abused. Article 42: the State shall make provision for just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief.
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Ledger POL03-I02 summarises Arts 38-39; this row quotes the gender limbs. Directive Principles are not enforceable by courts (Art 37, ledger POL03-I01).

claim: Article 51A(e): it is a Fundamental Duty of every citizen 'to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women'.
value: Art 51A(e)
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Ledger POL03-I07 lists all eleven duties; this is the gender duty (added by the 42nd Amendment per that row).

claim: Article 243D(3): not less than one-third of the seats in every Panchayat, including seats reserved for women of SC/ST, are reserved for women; 243D(4): offices of Chairpersons are reserved for SCs, STs and women as State law provides. Article 243T(3) gives the same one-third rule for Municipalities.
value: one-third of Panchayat and Municipal seats
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Constitution (73rd and 74th Amendment) rules, in the text as on 10 Sep 2026. Not quoted: percentage of women elected.

claim: 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), 2023: Art 330A reserves seats for women in the House of the People and Art 332A in State Legislative Assemblies, 'as nearly as may be' one-third of seats filled by direct election (including SC/ST women's seats); Art 239AA is amended likewise for Delhi. Art 334A makes it effective only after a delimitation exercise based on the first census taken after the Act's commencement, for fifteen years.
value: one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats; after delimitation; 15-year term
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice; and The Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, Gazette of India Extraordinary, 28 Sep 2023
second_source: The Gazette of India Extraordinary, 28 Sep 2023 (CG-DL-E-29092023-249053)
note: Commencement: the Act says it comes into force on a date the Centre appoints by notification (s.1(2)); the Constitution as on 10 Sep 2026 prints the footnote 'Ins. by the Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, s.3 (w.e.f. 16-4-2026)' (read on the rendered page; the text layer also carries an overlapping 'date yet to be notified'). The notification itself was not found. Art 334A: seats take effect only after delimitation, so women's seats are not yet in use in Parliament. Ledger POL03-C21 now CONFIRMED as to what the Legislative Department file prints, and warns that the text layer also says (date yet to be notified). [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Stale note corrected; Act ss.2-5 and Arts 330A/332A/334A read at the Gazette and Constitution PDF pages cited.

claim: Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (13 Aug 1997; Verma CJI, Sujata Manohar, B.N. Kirpal JJ.): in the absence of a law, the Court laid down guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace under Article 32, to be treated as law declared under Article 141; it read gender equality and the right to work with dignity in Arts 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21, and read in international conventions under Art 51(c). Guideline 7: a Complaints Committee headed by a woman, at least half its members women, with a third party such as an NGO.
value: guidelines until legislation; committee headed by a woman
source: Vishaka v State of Rajasthan, (1997) 6 SCC 241, via Indian Kanoon (mirror; Supreme Court copy not reached)
second_source: PIB Backgrounder 'Building Inclusive Workplaces', 13 Oct 2025 (Sexual Harassment Act 2013 requires Internal Complaints Committees)
note: Mirror copy. The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 replaced these guidelines; the PIB backgrounder describes the Act and its ICC rule (read), but India Code returned HTTP 504 for the Act's text, so the Act number, assent date (22 Apr 2013) and commencement (9 Dec 2013) seen in a search summary are UNVERIFIED.

claim: Joseph Shine v Union of India (27 Sep 2018; five judges: Misra CJI, Nariman, Khanwilkar, Chandrachud, Malhotra JJ.): s.497 IPC (adultery) held unconstitutional, and s.198 Cr.P.C., the complaint procedure for adultery, declared unconstitutional as well; Sowmithri Vishnu (1985) and V. Revathi (1988) overruled.
value: s.497 IPC struck down; s.198 CrPC; two earlier cases overruled
source: Joseph Shine v Union of India, via Indian Kanoon (mirror)
note: Mirror copy. Paragraph numbers are from the Chief Justice's opinion. The articles on which each judge relied were not tabulated here.

claim: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India (6 Sep 2018; five judges: Misra CJI, Nariman, Khanwilkar, Chandrachud, Malhotra JJ.): s.377 IPC, in so far as it criminalises consensual sexual conduct between adults of the same sex, is unconstitutional; Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013) is overruled; s.377 still governs non-consensual acts, acts with minors and bestiality.
value: consensual adult same-sex conduct decriminalised; Koushal overruled
source: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India, via Indian Kanoon (mirror) (Court copy also held: ../../2017-gs2-12/sources/navtej.pdf)
page_or_section: 'We hold and declare' passage; Malhotra J. conclusions (iii)-(iv)
second_source: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India, 6 Sep 2018, Supreme Court official copy
note: Mirror copy. Relevant to 'gender justice' only in the sense of sexual orientation and equal citizenship; do not overstate. Transgender rights (NALSA, 2014) were not read in this pass. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Content verified: Chandrachud J. "We hold and declare" (i),(v) PDF p.442; Misra CJI (xvii)-(xviii) pp.165-166; Malhotra J. conclusions (iii) minors/non-consensual/bestiality and (iv) Koushal overruled, pp.493-494. The Court copy is in the 2017-GS2-12 sources, so the mirror need not be relied on.

claim: Shayara Bano v Union of India (22 Aug 2017; five judges: Khehar CJI, Kurian Joseph, Nariman, Lalit, Nazeer JJ.): by a majority of 3:2 the practice of talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq) was set aside. One opinion (Nariman J., para 45) reasons that what is 'manifestly arbitrary' violates Article 14.
value: 3:2; triple talaq set aside
source: Shayara Bano v Union of India, via Indian Kanoon (mirror)
page_or_section: Order of the Court at the end; Nariman J. para 45
note: Mirror copy. The Order says only 'by a majority of 3:2'. Which three judges reasoned on which ground (Art 14 manifest arbitrariness v the practice not being essential to religion) was not tabulated; the attribution of para 45 to Nariman J. is from the opinion's position in the text, not from a header. The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 was not read.

claim: Anuj Garg v Hotel Association of India (6 Dec 2007; Sinha and Bedi JJ.): the Court dismissed the appeal and found no infirmity in the Delhi High Court's decision declaring s.30 of the Punjab Excise Act, 1914 (no 'woman' to be employed where liquor is consumed by the public) ultra vires Arts 14, 15 and 19(1)(g); it discussed 'romantic paternalism' as a ground of discrimination.
value: ban on women in bars not allowed
source: Anuj Garg v Hotel Association of India, (2008) 3 SCC 1, via Indian Kanoon (mirror)
note: Mirror copy. The High Court's declaration is described at para 3; the Supreme Court's conclusion is at para 55.

claim: Secretary, Ministry of Defence v Babita Puniya (17 Feb 2020; Chandrachud and Rastogi JJ.): women Short Service Commission officers in the Army must be considered for permanent commission in all ten streams where they are commissioned, irrespective of years served; the Court rejected arguments resting on 'sex stereotypes' about domestic obligations and physical strength; compliance within three months.
value: permanent commission for women SSC officers (all ten streams)
source: Secretary, Ministry of Defence v Babita Puniya, via Indian Kanoon (mirror)
note: Mirror copy. Paragraph numbers from the text near the quoted passages.

claim: Lt. Col. Nitisha v Union of India (25 Mar 2021; Chandrachud, Shah, Khanna JJ.): the Army's evaluation criteria for permanent commission, applied after Babita Puniya, were held to be systemic and indirect discrimination because facially neutral criteria (selective ACR evaluation, medical criteria) disproportionately affect women.
value: indirect discrimination recognised
source: Lt. Col. Nitisha v Union of India, via Indian Kanoon (mirror)
note: Mirror copy. Useful as the move from formal to substantive equality.

claim: Mary Roy v State of Kerala (24 Feb 1986; Bhagwati CJ and Pathak J.): Indian Christians in the former State of Travancore: the Travancore Christian Succession Act stood repealed on the Part-B States (Laws) Act, 1951 and intestate succession is governed by Chapter II of Part V of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 (daughters inherit equally with sons).
value: equal share for Christian daughters in the Travancore area
source: Mary Roy v State of Kerala, 1986 SCR (1) 371, via Indian Kanoon (mirror)
page_or_section: headnote and the paragraph 'We, therefore, allow the writ petitions'
note: Mirror copy. Often described as an Article 14 ruling; the Court decided on the statutes and said it was 'unnecessary to consider' whether the old Act's sections were unconstitutional. Say 'statutory ruling, equality in effect'.

claim: Independent Thought v Union of India (11 Oct 2017; Lokur and Gupta JJ.): Exception 2 to s.375 IPC was read down so that sexual intercourse by a man with his wife, the wife being under 18, is rape; the Court held the Exception arbitrary and violative of Arts 14, 15 and 21, discriminatory under Art 14, and inconsistent with POCSO; effect is prospective.
value: marital rape of a wife under 18 is rape
source: Independent Thought v Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 800, via Indian Kanoon (mirror)
page_or_section: Lokur J. paras 103-106 (reads Exception 2 as 'wife not being under eighteen years'; para 106 no view on marital rape of adult women); Gupta J. (concurring) paras 87-90: para 88 read down, Arts 14/15/21, POCSO, prospective; para 90 no view on marital rape
note: Mirror copy. Para 90: nothing in the judgment is an observation 'one way or the other' on marital rape (adult wives). [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Attribution corrected: paras 88-90 quoted in the old cite belong to Deepak Gupta J.'s separate concurring opinion, not the lead opinion of Lokur J. Both judges agree on the result.

claim: Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (11 Aug 2020; Mishra, Nazeer, Shah JJ.): under the substituted s.6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a daughter, born before or after the 2005 amendment, is a coparcener by birth in the same manner as a son with the same rights and liabilities; rights can be claimed from 9.9.2005, with savings for dispositions before 20 Dec 2004; the father need not have been alive on 9.9.2005.
value: daughters coparceners by birth
source: Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma, (2020) 9 SCC 1, via Indian Kanoon (mirror)
note: Mirror copy. Para 129(iii) was read to the words 'it is not necessary that father co...' and para 69 confirms the reasoning; the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 itself was not read at India Code.

claim: Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017: maternity leave raised from 12 to 26 weeks; employers with 50 or more employees must provide a crèche.
value: 26 weeks; crèche at 50+ employees
source: PIB Backgrounder 'Building Inclusive Workplaces', 13 Oct 2025; PIB (Ministry of Labour, Lok Sabha reply), 15 Jul 2019
page_or_section: 'Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (Amended 2017)'; Lok Sabha reply text
note: The Act's own text was not read (India Code unreachable). The 2025 PIB backgrounder also lists the Codes on Social Security; whether the 1961 Act has been subsumed in a Code now in force was not checked: say 'Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017' and nothing more about its current legal home.

claim: Female labour force participation: PIB (citing Ministry of Labour data) reports the female LFPR rose from 23.3% in 2017-18 to 41.7% in 2023-24 and the female worker-population ratio from 22% to 40.3%.
source: PIB Backgrounder 'Building Inclusive Workplaces', 13 Oct 2025 (Ministry of Labour and Employment data)
note: The underlying Periodic Labour Force Survey (MoSPI) tables were not read; this is the Government's own summary. The same page gives a monthly figure (female LFPR 33.7% in Aug 2025) on a different basis; do not mix the two series.

claim: Sabarimala (Indian Young Lawyers Association v State of Kerala, 28 Sep 2018), Sukanya Shantha (2024), transgender rights (NALSA 2014) and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019: not read or only partly read in this pass.
note: Gap check 10 Nov 2026: Sabarimala (2018) now read at the Court's own copy (claims -22 to -24). Still not read: NALSA (2014) at the Court's own copy (the old supremecourtofindia.nic.in/outtoday/wc40012.pdf link returns an HTML page, not the PDF; the sci.gov.in judis id or diary number was not found; Indian Kanoon mirror remains the only copy, see 2026-GS2-1-16); Sukanya Shantha (2024) not read; the 14 Nov 2019 reference to a larger bench after Sabarimala was not checked, so do not call the 2018 judgment 'final' without saying review petitions were filed (-24 gives the split only).

claim: POSH Act 2013, s.2(n): 'sexual harassment' includes any one or more unwelcome acts or behaviour, directly or by implication: (i) physical contact and advances; (ii) a demand or request for sexual favours; (iii) sexually coloured remarks; (iv) showing pornography; (v) any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of sexual nature.
value: s.2(n): five limbs
as_of: Act 14 of 2013; assent 22 Apr 2013; in force 9 Dec 2013
source: India Code (Legislative Department / Ministry of Women and Child Development), The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (Act 14 of 2013), s.2(n)
note: Read through India Code's data service on 2026-11-10 (central Act section record). Dates 22 Apr 2013 and 9 Dec 2013 are from the Act's India Code record (the record that carries them is filed under State listings but is the same Act number and title). Claim -06 gives Vishaka, which this Act replaced.

claim: POSH Act 2013, s.2(o): 'workplace' covers government bodies and bodies financed by them; private organisations carrying on commercial, professional, educational, health and other activities; hospitals and nursing homes; sports venues; and (clause v) any place visited by the employee arising out of or during employment. s.2(a)(ii) lets a woman employed in a dwelling place or house be an 'aggrieved woman', so domestic workers are covered.
value: s.2(o) wide workplace; domestic workers covered
source: India Code (Legislative Department / Ministry of Women and Child Development), The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (Act 14 of 2013), s.2(a), (o)
note: Clause (o)(v) in full: any place visited by the employee arising out of or during the course of employment including transportation by the employer for undertaking such journey; (o)(vi) adds a dwelling place or a house. Read 2026-11-10. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Stale note corrected after reading sources/indiacode_posh_s2.txt in full.

claim: POSH Act 2013, s.3(1): 'No woman shall be subjected to sexual harassment at any workplace.' s.3(2) lists circumstances that may amount to it: promise of preferential treatment; threat of detrimental treatment; threat about employment status; interference with work or creating an intimidating, offensive or hostile work environment; humiliating treatment likely to affect health or safety.
value: s.3(1) prohibition; s.3(2) five circumstances
source: India Code (Legislative Department / Ministry of Women and Child Development), The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (Act 14 of 2013), s.3
note: Read 2026-11-10. Quote under 15 words used for s.3(1).

claim: POSH Act 2013, s.4: every employer must by written order constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (at every office or unit); it has a Presiding Officer who is a senior woman employee, at least two employee members committed to women's causes or with social-work or legal experience, and one member from an NGO or a person familiar with sexual harassment issues; at least one-half of the members must be women. Members hold office for up to three years (s.4(3)).
value: ICC: woman Presiding Officer, one external member, at least half women
source: India Code (Legislative Department / Ministry of Women and Child Development), The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (Act 14 of 2013), s.4
note: Read 2026-11-10. s.6 (Local Committee, constituted by the District Officer) takes complaints from workplaces with fewer than ten workers or where the complaint is against the employer (sources/indiacode_posh_s6.txt). Whether the Act's s.9 three-month time limit has been changed by any later amendment was not checked; the text read is the India Code text.

claim: Sabarimala, Misra CJI (for himself and Khanwilkar J.), conclusions (iii)-(iv): Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965, excluding women aged 10 to 50, violates Hindu women's right to practise religion under Article 25(1) and makes it 'a dead letter'. Conclusion (v): 'public morality' in Art 25 is synonymous with constitutional morality. Conclusions (x)-(xii): Rule 3(b) is also ultra vires ss.3 and 4 of the 1965 Act.
value: Rule 3(b) struck; Art 25(1); constitutional morality
source: Indian Young Lawyers Association v State of Kerala, WP(C) 373 of 2006, judgment 28 Sep 2018, Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: para 144(iii)-(v), (x)-(xii), PDF pp.92-95 of the CJI opinion
note: Read in the Court's own copy on 2026-11-10 (PDF text layer). The petition was allowed (para 145). The four-to-one split is in claim -24. Nariman, Chandrachud and Malhotra JJ. wrote separately; their reasoning was not mined except Malhotra J.'s summary. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: p.96 is Nariman J.; para 145 is on p.95.

claim: Sabarimala was decided 4:1: Misra CJI and Khanwilkar J. in one opinion, Nariman J. and Chandrachud J. separately, and Indu Malhotra J. in dissent. Her summary: the petition 'does not deserve to be entertained for want of standing'; Art 14 'does not override' Art 25; Ayyappa worshippers plausibly are a religious denomination (Art 26); the matter is for a civil court on that point; Rule 3(b) is not ultra vires s.3 of the 1965 Act.
value: 4:1; Malhotra J. dissent: Art 14 v Art 25/26; constitutional morality
source: Indian Young Lawyers Association v State of Kerala, WP(C) 373 of 2006, judgment 28 Sep 2018, Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Malhotra J., para 16 summary (i)-(vi); judgments signed 28 Sep 2018
note: Read in the Court's own copy on 2026-11-10. The 4:1 count is from the four separate signatures and the one dissent; the Court's Order does not state a count in the text read. After this the Court received review petitions and referred questions to a larger bench in 2019 (not checked here).
